William Faulkner. The American modernist novelist who brought stream-of-consciousness and radical structural experimentation to the American South.

Born in New Albany, Mississippi in 1897, Faulkner moved to Oxford at age five and spent most of his life there despite travels and brief Hollywood screenwriting work. He created the fictional county of Yoknapatawpha as a microcosm of the region's history, violence, and moral complexity. He claimed to have fought in World War I and was influenced by Hemingway and other expatriate modernists, though unlike them, he chose to remain in the South. He explored themes of family decline and the South's relationship to its past—particularly slavery and the Civil War—with unprecedented moral seriousness and narrative complexity. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1949. His acceptance speech articulated a humanistic vision of literature that centered on the human heart in conflict with itself.

His major works include The Sound and the Fury, published in 1929. This four-part novel follows the Compson family across decades. The first three sections are told from perspectives of three sons—one intellectually disabled, one obsessed with his sister's sexuality, one bitter and resentful. The final section is told in third-person. Faulkner uses stream-of-consciousness, interior monologue, and fragmented time throughout. As I Lay Dying appeared in 1930. The novel consists of fifty-nine brief, stream-of-consciousness monologues from fifteen different characters about a dying mother and her family's journey to bury her. It is formally experimental and darkly comic. Absalom, Absalom! was published in 1936. This novel traces the history of Thomas Sutpen and his family across generations through multiple narrators' interpretations. It explores racism, pride, and the South's original sin. Light in August came out in 1932, offering interconnected narratives involving a pregnant woman, a light-skinned Black man, and a reverend, exploring alienation, sexuality, and racial identity.

Faulkner's method rests on stream of consciousness. He renders the unfiltered, digressive thoughts of characters as time loops and fragments. Consciousness itself becomes the primary subject. He employs multiple perspectives—the same events seen through different characters' eyes. Truth becomes plural and subjective; no omniscient narrator settles meaning. Southern Gothic aesthetics pervade his work: decay, grotesquerie, violence, and psychological darkness. The South's present is haunted by its past. His formal innovations include non-linear chronology, parenthetical asides, minimal punctuation, and stream-of-consciousness monologues that blur interior and exterior reality.

Faulkner brought modernist experimentation to American regional fiction, proving that the South and its traumas were fit subjects for the most demanding literary forms. His work forced American literature to confront slavery, racism, and the South's mythologized past through radical consciousness-exploration. He is less academic than Eliot, less linguistic than Joyce, but equally committed to rendering consciousness as the true subject of fiction. His influence flows through American fiction in writers like Flannery O'Connor and Carson McCullers, who inherit his use of stream-of-consciousness and Gothic Southern settings. He represents modernism's American wing: regional, psychologically intense, morally serious.
